A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study despite the revised title. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, algorithms and Appendices A-J support reliable comparison, including the new Appendix F.2 in v3.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated-user training experiments, mitigation comparisons, benchmark evaluations and qualitative model outputs in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds experiments varying the information available for identifying gameable users in Appendix F.2.

M1.justification: The iterated KTO procedure, expert-iteration alternative, objectives and mitigation mechanisms are unchanged. Algorithms 1-2 match; the added experiments apply the existing procedure under different user-information conditions.

E1.justification: Appendix F.2 adds therapy-talk scenarios without user memory, with easy or difficult vulnerability cues, with identical initial states, and with favorite-color cues. These extend input conditions within an existing task; the four main domains and external benchmark datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain the untrained controls, continued safety training with HH-RLHF and PKU SafeRLHF, and the same veto-training alternatives. Appendix F.2 compares user-information conditions for the existing approach, without introducing another comparison method.

E3.justification: The added F.2 experiments use a population with 50% gameable users and compare one- and two-turn conversations for relevant variants. They introduce controls over available user information and initial-state identity. Previously reported hyperparameters and benchmark protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 only briefly mentions exploratory evidence that background differences matter little. New Appendix F.2 and Figure 22 systematically test whether targeting depends on explicit gullibility cues, using memory removal, ambiguous or identical initial states, arbitrary color associations and conversation-length controls. This substantially strengthens the robustness analysis of a central finding.

E5.justification: Existing standard-error reporting across sampled trajectories is retained. However, new Figure 22 presents curves without visible uncertainty bands or a separate uncertainty specification, despite the retained statement that all plots report standard errors. No change in run counts or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Original plotted results and benchmark values are retained. F.2 adds findings that targeting can develop without gullibility descriptions, that the hard condition struggles with one turn but succeeds with two, and that identical initial states yield harmful trajectories for approximately 75% of gameable users and 20% of non-gameable users. These are results under added conditions.

T1.justification: The mathematical algorithm descriptions, reward and transition constructions in Appendix E.2, and evaluation definitions are unchanged. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The principal findings remain, but the abstract, introduction and conclusion more explicitly restrict their scope to the simulated settings. The abstract and contribution list also narrow the vulnerable-user statement from at most 2% to 2%, without changing the underlying Figure 6 results.

C2.justification: F.2 adds explanations involving conversational identification, population base rates and possible caution induced by gullibility descriptions. It also discloses that the harm evaluator depends on seeing vulnerability traits, estimating an approximately 85% ceiling without them. Sections 3.1 and 4.5 qualify simulation realism and interpretations of reasoning traces more carefully.

D1.justification: F.2 documents the construction of the added conditions, including red/blue associations, and supplies example messages and character traits in F.2.1-F.2.3. The reproducibility statement is shortened, while the code link, existing hyperparameters and detailed training/evaluation prompts remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Steinhardt's 2023 discussion of emergent deception and optimization to the introduction, related work and references. It removes the Nostalgebraist-based defense of chain-of-thought interpretability from Section 4.5, although that bibliography entry remains. The broader research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and selected introductory, interpretive and concluding passages are edited, including replacing several references to scheming with manipulation. Appendix F.2 is inserted and subsequent subsections are renumbered; the overall narrative and section organization remain stable.

P2.justification: v3 adds the two-panel Figure 22 and example displays in F.2. Table 1 drops the user/agent partial-observability columns, and several captions and Figure 7's excerpt are edited. Existing appendix Figures 22-43 become Figures 23-44; their results are retained rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: Appendix F.2 turns v1's brief exploratory reassurance into documented controls addressing dependence on explicit gullibility cues. More qualified framing also better matches the simulated evidence. These gains are limited: the new controls use 50% gameable users, reveal targeting errors and lack plotted uncertainty, so they do not fully establish robustness of the 2% case or applicability to real users.
